body:
What is a PUC certificate?

PUC stands for Pollution Under Control. A Pollution Under Control Certificate, often abbreviated as PUCC, records that a vehicle met the applicable prescribed emission limits during the specified in-use emissions test.

Vehicles can release smoke and harmful gases as they operate. Their emissions may change with use, wear and poor maintenance. A PUC test provides a practical check of selected emissions from a vehicle already in service.

In India, vehicle pollution requirements are governed by the Central Motor Vehicles Rules, 1989. The applicable standards and test methods depend on factors including fuel, vehicle type and the emission norms under which the vehicle was manufactured.

Which pollutants does an ordinary PUC test measure?

A very important distinction is that the routine PUC test does not measure every pollutant that a vehicle may produce.

Petrol, CNG and LPG vehicles

For vehicles operating on petrol, CNG or automotive LPG, routine exhaust testing primarily checks:

  • Carbon monoxide (CO): A poisonous gas associated with incomplete combustion. Its measured concentration is commonly expressed as a percentage.
  • Hydrocarbons (HC): Unburnt fuel-related compounds in the exhaust, commonly measured in parts per million (ppm). For idling tests, the rules estimate non-methane hydrocarbons (NMHC) for CNG as 0.3 × HC and reactive hydrocarbons (RHC) for LPG as 0.5 × HC, where HC is total hydrocarbon measured as n-hexane equivalent.

For certain petrol vehicles, including those covered by specified Bharat Stage requirements, testing may also include high-idle checks and the lambda value, which indicates the relationship between the air and fuel used for combustion. This additional measurement does not turn the routine PUC test into a complete analysis of every exhaust pollutant.

Diesel vehicles

Routine PUC testing of diesel vehicles primarily checks smoke density or opacity. The measurement indicates how much light is blocked by the smoke in the exhaust. This helps identify excessively smoky exhaust, which can be associated with soot and other particles.

Smoke opacity is not the same measurement as a direct laboratory determination of the mass of fine particulate matter. It also does not directly measure nitrogen oxides.

What is not directly measured in an ordinary PUC test?

Routine PUC testing should not be confused with a complete emissions assessment. In particular:

  • NOx: Ordinary tailpipe PUC testing does not directly quantify nitrogen oxides, even though vehicles may produce them.
  • CO2: The PUC certificate is not a direct measure of the vehicle's overall climate impact or total carbon dioxide emissions during real-world driving.
  • Fine particulate matter: A diesel smoke reading is not a direct measurement of all individual particle sizes or the total PM2.5 mass emitted during every driving condition.

PUC measurement distinction: Petrol, CNG and LPG vehicles are checked mainly for CO and HC, with other specified parameters where applicable. Diesel vehicles are checked mainly for exhaust smoke density. NOx is not a routine direct PUC measurement.

When is a PUC certificate required?

Rule 115(7) of the Central Motor Vehicles Rules provides that, after 1 year from the date of first registration, a motor vehicle must carry a valid PUC certificate issued by an agency authorised by the State Government.

The general validity period specified in the rule is 6 months. For vehicles manufactured according to BS-IV or BS-VI norms, the rule provides a validity period of 12 months.

The Ministry of Road Transport and Highways reiterated these periods in a statement dated 22 July 2021. It also identified the standardised certificate format notified on 14 June 2021 and the linkage of PUC records with the VAHAN vehicle database. These are the dated regulatory provisions used for this lesson as of the content cutoff of 3 November 2026.

A vehicle that exceeds the applicable limit may require maintenance or repair before it can pass the test. The precise numerical limits vary according to the relevant vehicle and emission category; one fixed CO or smoke limit should not be assumed for all vehicles.

PUC and Bharat Stage standards are different

Bharat Stage (BS) emission standards specify permissible emissions and related requirements for vehicles when they are manufactured and approved. The more advanced BS-VI framework addresses pollutants such as NOx and particulate emissions under prescribed vehicle approval requirements.

By contrast, PUC is a periodic check of selected emissions from a vehicle already in use. A vehicle's compliance with its Bharat Stage certification requirements does not remove the later PUC requirement.

Similarly, a valid PUC certificate means the vehicle passed the applicable test at that time. It does not establish that the vehicle emits no pollutants, remains compliant under every driving condition or has no effect on air quality.

Practical significance in Gujarat

The national PUC framework applies to vehicles registered and used in Gujarat. Authorised PUC centres conduct the applicable tests, while State transport authorities administer the certification and enforcement arrangements under the governing rules.

For a Gujarat learner, the crucial scientific distinction is between the substance tested and the substance that may still be present in exhaust. A diesel vehicle can pass a smoke test yet still produce NOx, because smoke opacity and nitrogen oxides are different emission measurements.

Prelims focus

  • PUC means Pollution Under Control; PUCC is the certificate.
  • Petrol, CNG and LPG vehicle testing primarily checks CO and HC.
  • Diesel vehicle testing primarily checks smoke density or opacity.
  • Ordinary PUC testing does not directly quantify NOx.
  • Under Rule 115(7), the PUC requirement applies after 1 year from first registration; the stated general validity is 6 months and BS-IV/BS-VI vehicle validity is 12 months.
  • Trap: Bharat Stage vehicle approval standards and an in-use PUC test are not identical.

[Ministry of Road Transport and Highways, Central Motor Vehicles Rules, 1989, Chapter V, Rule 115(2), petrol/CNG/LPG idling CO and HC standards and diesel smoke-density provisions, and Rule 115(7), PUC certification; Ministry of Road Transport and Highways, Government Standardises the Pollution Under Control Certificate Form to a Common Format, Press Information Bureau release ID 1737647, 22 July 2021, provisions on certificate validity and standardisation, consulted 3 November 2026; NCERT, Biology, Class 12, Environmental Issues, section 16.1.1, Controlling Vehicular Air Pollution.]

title: Pollution Under Control Certificates: Emission Measurements and Their Limits

body:
What are nitrogen oxides?

Nitrogen oxides, written collectively as NOx, are gaseous compounds containing nitrogen and oxygen. In basic vehicle-pollution studies, the most important examples are nitric oxide (NO) and nitrogen dioxide (NO2).

These gases must not be confused with ordinary nitrogen gas, N2, which forms most of the atmosphere. Nitrogen gas is relatively unreactive under normal conditions, whereas NOx gases participate in chemical reactions that contribute to air pollution.

How are NOx gases formed in vehicle engines?

Air entering a vehicle engine contains both nitrogen and oxygen. During combustion, temperatures can become high enough for these gases to react and form nitric oxide. Some nitric oxide later reacts with oxygen and other substances in the atmosphere to form nitrogen dioxide.

This is why NOx can be produced even when the fuel burns effectively. Unlike carbon monoxide, which is closely associated with incomplete combustion, nitrogen oxides are strongly associated with high-temperature combustion.

Road vehicles are an important source of NOx in urban environments. Other combustion sources, including thermal power plants and industrial activities, can also release nitrogen oxides.

Why is nitrogen dioxide harmful to health?

Nitrogen dioxide (NO2) is a reddish-brown gas at sufficiently high concentrations and is an important harmful component of NOx pollution. Breathing air containing elevated NO2 concentrations can irritate the respiratory tract.

Short-term exposure to high concentrations may produce or worsen symptoms such as:

  • Coughing and wheezing.
  • Difficulty breathing.
  • Inflammation and irritation of the airways.
  • Aggravation of asthma, especially in susceptible individuals.

Longer exposure to elevated concentrations may contribute to respiratory disease and may increase susceptibility to respiratory infections. Children, older people and individuals with asthma are among the groups at greater risk of adverse effects.

NO2 and CO act differently. NO2 mainly irritates and inflames the respiratory system. CO is particularly dangerous because it binds to haemoglobin and reduces the blood's oxygen-carrying capacity.

How does NOx contribute to air pollution?

Ground-level ozone and photochemical smog

In the presence of sunlight, nitrogen oxides participate in reactions involving volatile organic compounds. These reactions can form ground-level ozone (O3), an irritating air pollutant and an important component of photochemical smog.

Ground-level ozone should not be confused with the protective ozone layer in the upper atmosphere. Ozone high in the stratosphere helps absorb harmful ultraviolet radiation; ozone near the ground can damage health and vegetation.

Fine particles and reduced visibility

Nitrogen oxides can react with other atmospheric substances to form nitrate-containing secondary particles. These particles contribute to particulate air pollution and haze. Fine particles can penetrate the respiratory system when inhaled.

Acid rain

Nitrogen oxides can undergo reactions with oxygen, water and other substances in the atmosphere, producing nitric acid. When acidic substances are deposited through rain or other precipitation, they contribute to acid rain.

Acid rain can harm sensitive aquatic ecosystems, affect soils and vegetation, and contribute to the deterioration of certain building materials. Sulphur oxides are another important source of acid rain; nitrogen oxides are not its only cause.

How can vehicle-related NOx pollution be reduced?

Reducing vehicle-related NOx requires appropriate vehicle technology, functioning emission-control systems and proper maintenance. In petrol vehicles with suitable catalytic converters, nitrogen oxides can be converted mainly into nitrogen gas. Emission standards also require manufacturers to control pollutant releases from new vehicles.

Cleaner-burning fuels can help reduce some forms of pollution, but fuel substitution alone does not prove that NOx emissions have been eliminated. A CNG vehicle, for example, can still produce NOx because nitrogen and oxygen remain present in the air used for combustion.

Routine PUC testing is a further reason for careful interpretation. Passing a PUC test does not establish that a vehicle has emitted no NOx, because ordinary PUC testing does not directly measure that pollutant.

Distinguishing closely related chemical names

Formula or termMeaningPrincipal distinction
N2Nitrogen gasMain constituent of ordinary air
NONitric oxideImportant NOx gas formed during combustion
NO2Nitrogen dioxideHarmful respiratory irritant and NOx component
NOxCollective term for nitrogen oxidesIncludes NO and NO2 in vehicle-emission discussions
N2ONitrous oxideA distinct nitrogen compound and greenhouse gas

Nitrous oxide, N2O, is not another way of writing NO2. These compounds have different compositions and environmental roles. In ordinary vehicle-emission questions, NOx primarily directs attention to nitric oxide and nitrogen dioxide.

One-glance revision of fuels and vehicle emissions

The 4 central concepts in this subtopic concern different aspects of fuel use and pollution:

  • PNG and LPG: These are fuel-related terms. PNG is piped natural gas consisting mainly of methane; LPG is a propane–butane fuel stored in liquefied form.
  • E20: This describes the composition of ethanol-blended petrol: 20% ethanol and 80% petrol by volume.
  • PUC: This is an in-use vehicle emissions check. Petrol, CNG and LPG testing mainly concerns CO and HC; diesel testing mainly concerns smoke density.
  • NOx: These are nitrogen oxides associated with combustion, especially NO and NO2. They cause or contribute to respiratory harm, ground-level ozone, secondary particles and acid rain.

The distinctions fit together in a simple way. A vehicle may use a particular fuel, produce several pollutants while burning it, and undergo a PUC test that measures only selected emissions. The harmful properties of NOx must therefore be understood independently of both the fuel's name and the existence of a valid PUC certificate.

Prelims focus

  • NOx commonly includes NO and NO2 in vehicle-emission studies.
  • High-temperature combustion can form nitrogen oxides from nitrogen and oxygen.
  • NO2 can irritate airways and aggravate asthma.
  • NOx contributes to ground-level ozone and nitrate-containing fine particles.
  • Atmospheric reactions involving NOx can produce nitric acid and contribute to acid rain.
  • Trap: A vehicle with a valid routine PUC certificate may still emit NOx because the ordinary PUC test does not directly quantify it.

[NCERT, Science, Class 8, Pollution of Air and Water, sections 18.1–18.3, printed pp. 239–242, 2018–19 edition; NCERT, Science, Class 9, Natural Resources, section 14.1.4, Air Pollution; NCERT, Biology, Class 12, Environmental Issues, section 16.1.1, Controlling Vehicular Air Pollution; United States Environmental Protection Agency, Basic Information about NO2, sections on sources, health effects and environmental effects, page updated 24 June 2026, consulted 3 November 2026; Ministry of Road Transport and Highways, Central Motor Vehicles Rules, 1989, Chapter V, Rule 115(2), routine petrol/CNG/LPG and diesel emission-test provisions, consulted 3 November 2026.]
